newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JUNE 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JUNE 18.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--A Supreme Court ruling on the payment of compound interest that has reversed a two-decade old precedent has been referred to the full bench of the court. The ruling says that banks can only only impose compound interest on doebtors' loans if they agree on the manner of repayment.

--National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou may reveal the contents of the finance ministry's new bill on tax fines today. The bill foresees a favourable rescheduling of debts to the state.
--The Athens bourse suffered a surprising 2.94 percent fall at yesterday's session with the general price index closing below the 1,600 level.

--The success of the second Greek telecoms organisation's float will lead the way to stepped up privatisations, according to reports. Papandoniou is expected to announce the government's intentions in this sector after the summit in Amsterdam.
--Ten-year fixed coupon bonds will carry an interest rate of 8.9 percent with the rate for seven-year bonds rising to 9.0 percent.

--The impressive increase in the absorption rate of the public investment programme combined with a construction boom over the winter and increased wages in the private sector have created the conditions for increased demand and lower inflation, according to the finance ministry.
--Recent studies show that fewer firms were established in 1996 but those that were utilised a wider capital base in contrast to 1995.

--The message of the Amsterdam summit is that the euro will be a reality on January 1, 1999 and this obliges the Greek government to single-mindedly continue with its economic programme. The Amsterdam summit brought Greece recognition of external borders and the recognition of the particular problems of the islands.
--Government, union and employers will begin broaching the touchy subject of social insurance and pensions today when their "social dialogue" gets under way.

--The monopoly on telecommunications held by OTE may be abolished two years earlier than the time wanted by the government, if the European Commmission decides a three-year transitional period is adequate.
